what: A deep clone is a copy of a value where every nested object, array, Map and Set is copied too. Changing the copy never changes the original.
A normal copy such as { ...obj } is shallow: the top level is new, but nested objects are still shared. A deep clone walks the whole structure and builds a new container for each level.

Two things make this harder than it looks. Some values need special handling (Date, RegExp, Map, Set), and objects can point back to themselves (circular references). A WeakMap that remembers "original → copy" solves the second problem.
Think of photocopying a binder of linked pages. If page 3 says "see page 1", the copy must say "see copied page 1", not send you back to the original binder.

steps: If the value is a primitive, return it as it is. There is nothing to copy.
If you have already cloned this exact object, return the earlier copy from the WeakMap. This stops infinite loops and keeps shared references shared.
Pick the right way to build the empty copy: a new Date, a new RegExp, a new Map, a new Set, an array, or a plain object.
Register the new empty copy in the WeakMap before you fill it.
Clone every child with the same recursive function and put the results into the copy.
how.diagram:
a = { name: 'a' }; a.self = a

clone(a)        seen: {}
  new copy A'   seen: { a -> A' }      <- register first
  clone(a.self)
    a is in seen -> return A'
  A'.self = A'
Result: A'.self === A'  (not a)

where: State snapshots
Undo/redo and time-travel tools keep a full copy of the state before each change.
Safe mutation
Copy a config or form object, edit the copy freely, and keep the original untouched.
Worker messages
The built-in structuredClone does this job for messages between threads.
Not a fit
Class instances with private fields, DOM nodes and functions cannot be cloned by a simple walker. Very large graphs are also slow, so clone only what you need.

opts: { d: Date, u: undefined, n: NaN }, an exact copy
It throws a TypeError because of the Date
why: JSON has no Date type, so the date becomes an ISO string. undefined values are dropped, and NaN becomes null.
The trap is thinking JSON round-tripping is a deep clone. It only works for plain JSON data.

opts: It returns a copy where copy.me === copy
It throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
It returns {} because the loop skips cycles
why: clone(a) calls clone(a.me), which is clone(a) again. Nothing records that a was already visited, so the recursion never ends.
The trap is expecting JavaScript to detect cycles by itself. It does not.

opts: No. When the loop reaches a.me, a is not in seen yet, so it recurses forever
Yes. The WeakMap is filled before the function returns
No, because WeakMap cannot store objects as keys
why: The lookup happens at the start of every call. At that moment the outer call has not reached seen.set, so the lookup misses.
Register the empty copy first, then fill it. That is the whole trick.

think.q: The clone checks only typeof value === "object" and then calls Object.keys(value). What happens for deepClone({ a: null })?
opts: It throws a TypeError because Object.keys(null) is invalid
why: typeof null is "object", an old quirk of JavaScript. The check lets null through and Object.keys(null) throws.
Always test value === null together with the typeof check.
Both p and q pointed to the same object, so the WeakMap returns the same copy for both. The copy keeps the original sharing structure (c.p === c.q), but it is a new object (c.p !== shared).
A clone without the WeakMap would create two separate copies and quietly change the shape of the data.

problems.pseudo:
deepClone(value, seen = empty weak map)
  if value is not an object (or is null)
    if it is a function, return nothing
    otherwise return the value itself
  if seen already has value
    return the stored copy
  if value is a Date
    return a new Date with the same time
  if value is a RegExp
    return a new RegExp with the same source and flags
  if value is a Map
    make an empty Map, store it in seen
    for each entry, clone the key and the value, add them
    return it
  if value is a Set
    same idea with items
  if value is an array
    make an empty array, store it in seen
    clone each item into the same position
    return it
  otherwise it is a plain object
    make an empty object with the same prototype, store it in seen
    for each own key, clone the value
    skip keys whose value is a function
    return it
  // bonus: copy symbol keys too
watch: At which exact moment do you save the new empty copy in the WeakMap, and why does the order matter?
How do you tell null, arrays, Dates and plain objects apart, given that typeof says "object" for all of them?
If two properties point to the same object, should the copy contain one object or two?

build.problem: Implement deepClone(value) that copies primitives, arrays, plain objects, Date, RegExp, Map, Set and circular references, without using JSON.stringify.
reqs: Return primitives as they are.
Clone arrays and plain objects recursively, with no shared nested references.
Copy Date and RegExp (keep the time, source and flags).
Clone Map and Set, including their object keys and values.
Handle circular references with a WeakMap, and keep shared references shared.
Skip function-valued properties.

checks.t: Nested objects and arrays are fully independent
checks.gap: You are probably copying only the top level. Recurse into every child that is an object or array, and assign the cloned child, not the original.

checks.t: Date is copied as a real Date
checks.test:
const d = new Date(1e12); const c = deepClone({ d });
console.log(c.d instanceof Date, c.d !== d, c.d.getTime() === d.getTime()); // expected: true true true
checks.gap: A Date has no own enumerable keys, so a plain-object walk turns it into {}. Check instanceof Date first and build new Date(original.getTime()).

checks.t: RegExp keeps its source and flags
checks.test:
const r = /a+/gi; const c = deepClone(r);
console.log(c !== r, c.source, c.flags); // expected: true a+ gi
checks.verify:
const r = /a+/gi; const c = deepClone(r);
assert(c !== r && c instanceof RegExp, 'must be a new RegExp'); assert(c.source === 'a+' && c.flags === 'gi', 'source and flags must match')
checks.gap: Create the copy with new RegExp(r.source, r.flags). Walking its keys gives an empty object.

checks.t: Map and Set contents are cloned, not shared
checks.gap: Map and Set keep their data in internal slots, so Object.keys sees nothing. Create a new Map or Set and add cloned entries one by one.

checks.t: Circular references do not crash and stay circular
checks.verify:
const a = { name: 'a' }; a.self = a; const c = deepClone(a);
assert(c !== a, 'must be a new object'); assert(c.self === c, 'the cycle must point to the copy, not the original'); assert(c.name === 'a', 'values copied')
checks.gap: Save the new empty copy in the WeakMap before cloning its children, and look in the WeakMap at the start of every call.

checks.t: Shared references stay shared inside the copy
checks.test:
const shared = { n: 1 }; const c = deepClone({ p: shared, q: shared });
console.log(c.p === c.q, c.p !== shared); // expected: true true
checks.verify:
const shared = { n: 1 }; const c = deepClone({ p: shared, q: shared });
assert(c.p === c.q, 'p and q must be the same copied object'); assert(c.p !== shared, 'must not point to the original')
checks.gap: If your WeakMap stores every visited object (not only on cycles), the second visit returns the same copy automatically. Make sure you save objects when you first clone them.

checks.t: Function-valued properties are skipped
checks.test:
const c = deepClone({ f() {}, n: 1 });
console.log('f' in c, c.n); // expected: false 1
checks.verify:
const c = deepClone({ f() {}, n: 1 });
assert(!('f' in c), 'function property must be skipped'); assert(c.n === 1, 'other values copied')
checks.gap: Check typeof value === "function" and skip the key (or return undefined for a top-level function) instead of copying the reference.

notes: Primitives and null are the base case. Check null explicitly because typeof null is "object".
The WeakMap records "original → copy". It breaks cycles and keeps shared references shared.
Register the empty copy before filling it, otherwise a child that points back to the parent cannot find it.
Special objects (Date, RegExp, Map, Set) keep data in internal slots, so each needs its own constructor call.
For production code, prefer the built-in structuredClone. It handles these cases, but it throws on functions.
next: Also copy Symbol keys and property descriptors (getters and setters).
Support typed arrays, Error objects and Boolean/Number/String wrapper objects.
Write deepEqual(a, b) that handles the same set of types and cycles.

what: once(fn) returns a new function. The first time you call it, it runs fn and remembers the result. Every later call skips fn and returns that remembered result.
The wrapper needs two pieces of memory that survive between calls: "did I run already?" and "what was the result?". A closure keeps both alive without any global variable.
Think of a one-time password. The first use works. After that, the system just tells you "already used" and never opens the door again.

steps: Create two variables in the outer function: a called flag and a result slot.
Return a wrapper function that accepts any arguments.
On the first call: set the flag, run the original function with the same this and arguments, and store what it returns.
On every call: return the stored result. Later arguments are ignored.
Optional: attach a reset() method that clears the flag and result.
how.diagram:
const init = once(connect)

init(1)   called=false -> run connect(1) -> result R, called=true -> R
init(2)   called=true  -> skip          -> R
init(3)   called=true  -> skip          -> R

init.reset()  -> called=false, result=undefined
init(4)   runs connect(4) again

where: Initialisation
Open a database connection or load a config file once, even if many parts of the page ask for it.
Event handlers
Make sure a "submit" or "pay" action cannot run twice if a user double-clicks.
Lazy setup
Create an expensive object the first time it is needed, then reuse it.
Watch out
If fn is async, you cache the promise, not the final value. Also, a call that throws is still counted as the one call.

think.q:
const double = once((x) => x * 2)
console.log(double(2), double(5))
What is printed?
why: The first call runs with 2 and caches 4. The second call does not run fn, so the argument 5 is ignored and the cached 4 comes back.
The trap is thinking the wrapper recomputes with new arguments. It only remembers.

think.q:
function once(fn) {
  return function (...args) {
    let called = false
    let result
    if (!called) {
      called = true
      result = fn(...args)
    }
    return result
  }
}
If you call the wrapper three times, how many times does fn run?
opts: 3 times, because called is created fresh on every call
2 times, the first and the last
why: The variables live inside the returned function, so each call gets its own new called = false. The memory does not survive between calls.
The flag must be declared in the outer function, so every call shares it through the closure.

think.q:
The wrapper calls the original with fn(...args) instead of fn.apply(this, args). In strict-mode code, what happens here?
const o = { n: 1, get: once(function () { return this.n }) }
o.get()
opts: It throws a TypeError, because this is undefined inside fn
why: A plain call fn(...args) has no object in front of it, so this is lost. In strict mode that means undefined, and this.n throws.
Use fn.apply(this, args) inside a normal function wrapper. An arrow function wrapper would also lose the caller's this.

opts: 3 times, because 0 is falsy so the cache looks empty
why: The guard checks the value, not whether a call happened. A result of 0, "", false or undefined looks "not cached", so fn runs again.
Use a separate boolean flag. It says "I already ran" no matter what the result was.

think.q:
const f = once((x) => x + 1)
f(1)
f.reset()
console.log(f(10))
why: reset() clears the flag and the stored result, so the next call behaves like a first call. It runs with 10 and returns 11.
If reset forgot to clear the flag, you would get the old 2.

problems.pseudo:
once(fn)
  remember "called" = false
  remember "result" = nothing
  create wrapper(any arguments)
    if called is false
      set called to true
      run fn with the wrapper's own "this" and the same arguments
      save what it returns as result
    return result
  give the wrapper a reset action
    set called to false
    clear the result
  return the wrapper
watch: Where do called and result live, so they survive from one call to the next?
What if the result is 0, false or undefined? Can your check still tell that the function already ran?
Which this does the original function see when the wrapper is used as a method?

build.problem: Implement once(fn) that returns a wrapper running fn only on the first call and returning the same result afterwards.
reqs: Run fn only on the first call.
Later calls return the first result without running fn.
Pass all arguments and the correct this on the first call.
Cache results that are falsy, including undefined.
Bonus: add a reset() method on the wrapper.

checks.t: The first call runs fn and returns its value
checks.test:
let n = 0; const f = once(() => { n++; return 'hi' });
console.log(f(), n); // expected: hi 1
checks.verify:
let n = 0; const f = once(() => { n++; return 'hi' });
assert(f() === 'hi' && n === 1, 'first call must run fn and return its value')
checks.gap: On the first call you must run fn and return its result. Check that you return the value on every path.

checks.t: Later calls return the cached value and do not run fn
checks.test:
let n = 0; const f = once((x) => { n++; return x * 2 });
console.log(f(2), f(5), f(9), n); // expected: 4 4 4 1
checks.verify:
let n = 0; const f = once((x) => { n++; return x * 2 });
assert(f(2) === 4 && f(5) === 4 && f(9) === 4, 'must return the first result'); assert(n === 1, 'fn must run once')
checks.gap: The flag and result must live in the outer function (the closure). If you declare them inside the wrapper, each call starts fresh.

checks.t: All arguments reach fn on the first call
checks.test:
const f = once((...a) => a.join('-'));
console.log(f(1, 2, 3)); // expected: 1-2-3
checks.verify:
const f = once((...a) => a.join('-'));
assert(f(1, 2, 3) === '1-2-3', 'all arguments must be passed')
checks.gap: Use a rest parameter (...args) and spread or apply them. Do not hard-code one argument.

checks.t: The caller's this is preserved
checks.test:
const o = { v: 7, get: once(function () { return this.v }) };
console.log(o.get()); // expected: 7
checks.verify:
const o = { v: 7, get: once(function () { return this.v }) };
assert(o.get() === 7, 'this must be the object the method was called on')
checks.gap: The wrapper must be a normal function (not an arrow) and call fn.apply(this, args) so this is forwarded.

checks.t: Falsy and undefined results are cached too
checks.verify:
let n = 0; const f = once(() => { n++; return 0 }); f(); f(); f();
assert(n === 1, 'a falsy result must not trigger another call'); let m = 0; const g = once(() => { m++ }); g(); g(); assert(m === 1, 'undefined result must be cached too')
checks.gap: Do not use the result to decide whether to run. Keep a separate boolean called flag.

checks.t: reset() lets the function run again
checks.gap: Attach reset to the wrapper function object and clear both the flag and the cached result.

notes: The closure holds called and result, so state survives between calls with no globals.
A separate boolean flag is safer than checking the result, because any value (even undefined) can be a valid result.
fn.apply(this, args) forwards the caller's this and all arguments.
A normal function is needed for the wrapper so that this is the caller. An arrow function would capture the outer this instead.
next: Write before(n, fn) that runs fn for the first n - 1 calls and then caches the last result.
Make once work for async functions so that parallel callers share one promise.
Decide what should happen if fn throws: cache the error, or allow a retry?

what: groupBy(array, key) sorts the items of an array into labelled buckets. It returns an object where each property name is a group label, and each value is the array of items in that group.
The key can be a property name such as "role", or a function that computes the label, such as (u) => u.age > 30 ? "senior" : "junior". In both cases you get one label per item.
Think of sorting laundry into baskets by colour. Each shirt goes into exactly one basket, and the baskets are created the first time you need them.

steps: Decide how to get a label: call the function, or read the property.
Start with an empty result object.
For each item, compute its label.
If the result has no bucket for that label yet, create an empty array.
Push the item into the bucket. Return the result object at the end.
how.diagram:
users, key = "role"
 {ann, admin}  -> admin: [ann]
 {bob, user}   -> user:  [bob]
 {cy,  admin}  -> admin: [ann, cy]

result = { admin: [ann, cy], user: [bob] }

where: Tables and lists
Show orders grouped by status, or contacts grouped by first letter.
Analytics
Count events per day or per page by grouping first, then taking each bucket's length.
Data prep
Group API rows by an id before building a nested UI.
Watch out
Labels become string property names. 1 and "1" land in the same bucket, and keys like "constructor" can clash with built-in names.

think.q:
const r = groupBy([6.1, 4.2, 6.3], Math.floor)
console.log(Object.keys(r))
why: Object keys are always strings, so the numbers become "6" and "4". Integer-like keys are also listed in ascending numeric order, not in insertion order.
The trap is expecting the order of first appearance. If order matters, use a Map.

think.q:
The accumulator is a normal {}:
acc[k] = acc[k] || []
acc[k].push(item)
What happens for groupBy([{ t: "constructor" }], "t")?
opts: It returns {} because the key is reserved
It throws a TypeError, because acc.constructor is the Object function, so it is not replaced and has no push
why: A normal object inherits properties like constructor and toString. acc["constructor"] is already truthy, so the code skips creating an array and calls push on a function.
Use Object.create(null) for the accumulator, or check with Object.hasOwn.

think.q:
groupBy([{ a: 1 }, { b: 2 }], "a")
What are the keys of the result?
opts: ["1"], because items without the key are skipped
It throws, because the second item has no a
why: Reading a missing property gives undefined, and using it as a key turns it into the string "undefined". The second item goes into that bucket.
This is the behaviour the task asks for. You can change it later if you prefer to skip those items.

think.q:
const users = [{ name: "Ann", role: "admin" }]
const g = groupBy(users, "role")
console.log(g.admin[0] === users[0])
opts: true, because the buckets hold the same object references
why: Grouping only moves references into new arrays. The objects themselves are not copied, so changing g.admin[0].name also changes users[0].
The original array is not changed, which is what "no mutation" means here.

problems.pseudo:
groupBy(array, key)
  decide how to read a label from an item
    if key is a function, call it with the item
    otherwise read the property named by key
  create an empty result with no inherited properties
  for each item in the array
    compute its label
    if the result has no bucket for that label
      create an empty list for it
    add the item to that list
  return the result
  // bonus: also pass the index to a function key
watch: What type are the labels in the final object, even if your function returns numbers?
What does a missing property give you, and which bucket does it end up in?
Could a label like "constructor" collide with something the result object already has?

build.problem: Implement groupBy(array, key) where key is a property name or a function, returning an object that maps each label to an array of items.
reqs: Support a string key such as "role".
Support a function key such as (u) => u.age > 30 ? "senior" : "junior".
Keep the original items and their order, and do not mutate the input array.
Return an empty object for an empty array.
Items with a missing key go under "undefined".

checks.t: Groups by a string property
checks.verify:
const u = [{ n: 'a', r: 'x' }, { n: 'b', r: 'y' }, { n: 'c', r: 'x' }]; const g = groupBy(u, 'r');
assert(g.x.map(i => i.n).join() === 'a,c' && g.y.length === 1, 'must group by property and keep order')
checks.gap: Read the label with item[key] and push the item into result[label]. Create the array the first time a label appears.

checks.t: Groups by a function
checks.test:
const g = groupBy([20, 35, 50], n => n > 30 ? 'senior' : 'junior');
console.log(g.junior, g.senior); // expected: [20] [35, 50]
checks.verify:
const g = groupBy([20, 35, 50], n => n > 30 ? 'senior' : 'junior');
assert(g.junior.length === 1 && g.junior[0] === 20 && g.senior.length === 2, 'must group by function result')
checks.gap: Check typeof key === "function" and call key(item) to get the label instead of reading a property.

checks.t: Items are the same objects and the input is not changed
checks.test:
const u = [{ r: 'x' }]; const g = groupBy(u, 'r');
console.log(g.x[0] === u[0], u.length); // expected: true 1
checks.verify:
const u = [{ r: 'x' }]; const g = groupBy(u, 'r');
assert(g.x[0] === u[0], 'items must be the same references'); assert(u.length === 1 && u[0].r === 'x', 'input must not change')
checks.gap: Push the original item, not a copy, and never splice or pop from the input array.

checks.t: An empty array gives an empty object
checks.test: console.log(Object.keys(groupBy([], 'r')).length); // expected: 0
checks.verify: assert(Object.keys(groupBy([], 'r')).length === 0, 'empty input must give empty result')
checks.gap: Start from an empty object and return it even when the loop never runs. Do not return null or undefined.

checks.t: A missing key goes under "undefined"
checks.test:
const g = groupBy([{ a: 1 }, { b: 2 }], 'a');
console.log(Object.keys(g).join()); // expected: 1,undefined
checks.verify:
const g = groupBy([{ a: 1 }, { b: 2 }], 'a');
assert(g['1'].length === 1 && g['undefined'].length === 1, 'missing key must be grouped under undefined')
checks.gap: Do not skip items whose label is undefined. Using it as an object key already produces the string "undefined".

checks.t: Labels that match built-in names still work
checks.test:
const g = groupBy([{ t: 'constructor' }, { t: 'toString' }], 't');
console.log(g.constructor.length, g.toString.length); // expected: 1 1
checks.gap: A plain {} already has constructor and toString. Create the result with Object.create(null) (or check with Object.hasOwn).

notes: One label per item, then "create bucket if missing, push item". That is the whole algorithm.
Object keys are strings, so numeric labels become strings and integer-like keys are ordered numerically.
Object.create(null) gives an object with no inherited names, so a label like "constructor" is safe.
Items are placed by reference. The input array and its items are not changed.
You can write this with reduce. A plain loop is easier to read for beginners.
next: Return a Map instead, so non-string labels and insertion order are kept.
Add countBy(array, key) that returns how many items are in each group.
Compare with the built-in Object.groupBy and list the differences.

problems.signature: myMap(arr, fn) · myFilter(arr, fn) · myReduce(arr, fn, initialValue?)

what: map, filter and reduce are the three workhorses of array code. Each walks through an array and calls your callback for every item. map builds a new array of results, filter keeps the items you approve, and reduce folds everything into one value.

Writing them yourself shows what the callback receives: (item, index, array). It also shows the details that people forget, such as what reduce does when there is no starting value, and that the built-ins skip empty slots in sparse arrays.
Think of an assembly line. map changes each product, filter removes the faulty ones, and reduce packs everything into a single box.

steps: Check the callback first. If it is not a function, throw a TypeError.
myMap: make a result array of the same length. For each existing item, store callback(item, index, array) at the same index.
myFilter: make an empty result. For each existing item, push it only if the callback returns a truthy value.
myReduce: keep an accumulator. Use the initial value if one was given, otherwise take the first existing item and start from the next one. Replace the accumulator with each callback result.
An empty array with no initial value has nothing to start from, so myReduce throws a TypeError.
how.diagram:
myReduce([1, 2, 3], add)         (no initial value)
 acc = 1        start at index 1
 acc = add(1, 2) = 3
 acc = add(3, 3) = 6        -> 6

myReduce([1, 2, 3], add, 10)     (initial value)
 acc = 10       start at index 0
 10 -> 11 -> 13 -> 16       -> 16

where: UI lists
map turns data into rows or components, and filter removes items that should not be shown.
Totals
reduce sums prices, counts items by type, or builds a lookup object.
Pipelines
Chain them: filter the active users, map them to names, reduce them to a count.
Watch out
Chaining many of them walks the array many times. For very large arrays, one reduce or a single loop can be faster.

think.q: console.log(["1", "2", "3"].map(parseInt))
why: map calls the callback as (item, index, array). So parseInt receives the index as its second argument, the radix: parseInt("2", 1) and parseInt("3", 2) are NaN.
This is why your myMap must pass the index. It is also why you should wrap such callbacks: (x) => parseInt(x).

think.q:
A custom reduce decides "no initial value" with if (initialValue === undefined). What goes wrong with this call?
[].reduce((a, b) => a + b, undefined)
opts: The built-in returns undefined, but this custom version throws, because it cannot tell "no value" from "undefined was passed"
The built-in throws, the custom version returns undefined
why: Passing undefined explicitly is still "an initial value was given". The built-in checks how many arguments were passed, not what their value is.
Use arguments.length (or a rest parameter) to know whether the third argument exists.
Without an initial value, the first item becomes the accumulator, and the loop starts at index 1. With three items that means only two callbacks: 1 + 2, then 3 + 3.
If you always start at index 0, you call the callback one time too many.

opts: It throws, because i is not defined
why: The callback is called with only the item, so its second parameter i is undefined. The result is [undefined, undefined].
Use an indexed loop and call fn(arr[i], i, arr).

think.q:
What does the built-in map do here?
let calls = 0
const r = [1, , 3].map((x) => { calls++; return x * 2 })
opts: calls is 2 and r keeps the empty slot: [2, empty, 6]
why: Array methods skip holes in sparse arrays. The callback is not called for the empty slot, and map keeps the hole at the same index, so the length stays 3.
Test it with index in arr before calling the callback.

problems.pseudo:
check the callback
  if it is not a function, throw a TypeError

myMap(arr, fn)
  make a result list with the same length as arr
  for each position i from the start to the end
    if arr has a real item at i
      store fn(item, i, arr) at position i in the result
  return the result

myFilter(arr, fn)
  make an empty result list
  for each position i
    if arr has a real item at i
      if fn(item, i, arr) is truthy, add the item to the result
  return the result

myReduce(arr, fn, initialValue)
  if an initial value was passed (even undefined)
    accumulator = initial value, start at position 0
  otherwise
    find the first real item, use it as the accumulator
    if there is none, throw a TypeError
    start after it
  for each remaining real item
    accumulator = fn(accumulator, item, i, arr)
  return the accumulator
watch: Which three values does the callback receive, and in which order?
How do you know that an initial value was passed, when the caller might pass undefined on purpose?
What should happen for an empty slot in the array?

build.problem: Implement myMap, myFilter and myReduce as standalone functions (myMap(arr, fn) and so on) without using the built-in map, filter or reduce.
reqs: myMap returns a new array of fn(item, index, array) results.
myFilter returns a new array of items for which fn returns a truthy value.
myReduce uses the first item as the start when no initial value is passed.
All three pass (item, index, array) to the callback and do not change the input.
Throw a TypeError if the callback is not a function, and for an empty array in myReduce with no initial value.
Bonus: skip empty slots in sparse arrays like the built-ins.

checks.t: myMap passes (item, index, array) and returns a new array
checks.verify:
const a = ['a', 'b']; const r = myMap(a, (x, i, arr) => x + i + (arr === a));
assert(r.length === 2 && r[0] === 'a0true' && r[1] === 'b1true', 'callback must get item, index, array'); assert(r !== a, 'must return a new array')
checks.gap: Use an indexed loop and call fn(arr[i], i, arr). Calling fn(item) leaves the index and array as undefined.

checks.t: myMap does not change the input
checks.test:
const a = [1, 2, 3]; myMap(a, x => x * 2);
console.log(a); // expected: [1, 2, 3]
checks.verify:
const a = [1, 2, 3]; const r = myMap(a, x => x * 2);
assert(a.join() === '1,2,3', 'input must stay the same'); assert(r.join() === '2,4,6', 'result must be doubled')
checks.gap: Write results into a separate output array. Never assign back into arr[i].

checks.t: myFilter keeps items with a truthy result
checks.test:
const r = myFilter([1, 2, 3, 4], (x, i) => x % 2 === 0 || i === 0);
console.log(r); // expected: [1, 2, 4]
checks.verify:
const r = myFilter([1, 2, 3, 4], (x, i) => x % 2 === 0 || i === 0);
assert(r.join() === '1,2,4', 'must keep truthy results and pass the index'); assert(myFilter([], () => true).length === 0, 'empty in, empty out')
checks.gap: Push the original item (not the callback result) when the callback returns a truthy value.

checks.t: myReduce with an initial value
checks.test: console.log(myReduce([1, 2, 3], (a, x) => a + x, 10)); // expected: 16
checks.gap: With an initial value the accumulator starts as that value and the loop starts at index 0.

checks.t: Without an initial value, the first item starts it and the loop begins at index 1
checks.verify:
let calls = 0; const r = myReduce([1, 2, 3], (a, x) => { calls++; return a + x });
assert(r === 6 && calls === 2, 'must start at index 1 and call the callback twice')
checks.gap: When there is no initial value, set acc = arr[0] and begin the loop at index 1. Starting at 0 calls the callback once too often.

checks.t: An explicit undefined counts as an initial value; empty without one throws
checks.verify:
assert(myReduce([], (a, x) => a + x, undefined) === undefined, 'explicit undefined is an initial value');
let threw = false; try { myReduce([], (a, x) => a + x) } catch (e) { threw = e instanceof TypeError } assert(threw, 'empty array without initial value must throw TypeError')
checks.gap: Do not test the value of initialValue. Count the arguments (arguments.length or a rest parameter) to know whether it was passed.

checks.t: A non-function callback throws a TypeError
checks.gap: Add if (typeof fn !== "function") throw new TypeError(...) at the very top of each function.

notes: All three share one shape: validate the callback, loop by index, and call it with (item, index, array).
myMap allocates the result with the input length, so holes stay holes.
myFilter pushes the original item, not the callback result.
myReduce reads arguments.length because "no initial value" is different from "initial value is undefined".
The i in arr check makes the functions skip holes in sparse arrays, like the built-ins.
next: Add them as Array.prototype.myMap and so on, so that this is the array.

what: bind takes a function and gives you a new function with two things locked in: the value of this, and optionally the first few arguments. The original function is not called yet.

Locking this fixes the classic problem of a method losing its object when you pass it around as a callback. Locking arguments is called partial application: add.bind(null, 1) is a new function that already has 1 as its first argument.
There is one special rule. If you call a bound function with new, the locked this is ignored, and the new object is used instead.
Think of a phone with a speed-dial button. Pressing it always calls the same person (this), and you can also pre-type the first digits (partial arguments).

steps: Remember the original function (this inside myBind), the locked thisArg and the partial arguments.
Return a new function. When it is called, join the partial arguments with the new arguments, partials first.
For a normal call, run the original with the locked this and the joined arguments.
For a call with new, ignore the locked this. Construct a new object from the original function with the joined arguments.
Return whatever the original returns.
how.diagram:
const b = add.myBind(ctx, 1, 2)

b(3, 4)
  args = [1, 2] + [3, 4] = [1, 2, 3, 4]
  call:  add with this = ctx, args

new b(3, 4)
  this is ignored
  build a new object from add, args [1, 2, 3, 4]

where: Event handlers
Pass this.handleClick.bind(this) in older class components so the method keeps its instance.
Partial application
Create double = multiply.bind(null, 2) from a general function.
Borrowing methods
Call a method of one object on another, with the right this.
Not a fit
Arrow functions ignore bind for this, because they use the this of the place where they were written.

think.q:
function who() { return this.name }
const a = { name: "A" }
const b = { name: "B" }
console.log(who.bind(a).bind(b)())
why: The first bind locks this to a. The second bind wraps the already bound function, and its this is thrown away by the first one.
A bound function's this cannot be changed again, not even with call or apply.

think.q:
function P() { this.k = 1 }
const B = P.bind({ k: 99 })
console.log(new B().k)
opts: It throws, because a bound function cannot be used with new
why: With new, the locked this ({ k: 99 }) is ignored. A brand new object is created and P sets k to 1 on it.
This is the behaviour your myBind has to copy. A version that always uses apply(thisArg, ...) would return the wrong object.

think.q:
Function.prototype.myBind = function (ctx, ...partials) {
  return function (...args) {
    return this.apply(ctx, [...partials, ...args])
  }
}
Why does sayHi.myBind(user)() fail?
opts: Partials must come after the new arguments
The spread syntax is not allowed here
Inside the inner function, this is not the original function. It is whatever the call site gives, so this.apply breaks
why: this inside myBind is the original function, but the inner regular function gets its own this when it is called. With a plain call, this is undefined or the global object.
Save the original in a variable, for example const target = this, and use target inside.

think.q:
let n = 1
function show(x) { return x }
const b = show.bind(null, n)
n = 2
console.log(b())
why: Partial arguments are evaluated and stored at the moment you call bind. The value 1 was copied, so changing n later does not matter.
If you bind an object, the reference is stored, so changes inside that object are visible later.

problems.pseudo:
myBind(thisArg, ...partials)
  if the thing being bound is not a function, throw a TypeError
  remember the original function
  create a bound function that takes any new arguments
    join the partial arguments with the new arguments, partials first
    if it was called with "new"
      create a new object from the original function with the joined arguments
        (the locked "this" is ignored)
      return that object
    otherwise
      call the original with the locked "this" and the joined arguments
      return its result
  return the bound function
  // bonus: make sure new objects still pass "instanceof original"
watch: Inside your returned function, how do you still reach the original function?
How can the bound function tell that it was called with new?
Do the partial arguments stay the same for every call of the bound function?

reqs: Return a new function that calls the original with this fixed to thisArg.
Support partial application: f.myBind(ctx, a, b)(c, d) calls f with a, b, c, d.
Do not call the original at bind time.
When the bound function is called with new, ignore the bound this and create an instance of the original.
Instances made with new must be instanceof the original function.

checks.t: this is fixed, even with call or a detached call
checks.verify:
function get() { return this.v } const b = get.myBind({ v: 42 });
assert(b() === 42, 'bound this must be used'); assert(b.call({ v: 9 }) === 42, 'call must not override the bound this')
checks.gap: Always call the original with target.apply(thisArg, args). Never use the this of the bound function for a normal call.

checks.t: Partial arguments come first, then the new arguments
checks.test:
function add(a, b, c, d) { return [a, b, c, d].join('-') }
console.log(add.myBind(null, 1, 2)(3, 4)); // expected: 1-2-3-4
checks.verify:
function add(a, b, c, d) { return [a, b, c, d].join('-') }
assert(add.myBind(null, 1, 2)(3, 4) === '1-2-3-4', 'partials must be prepended')
checks.gap: Build the final list as partials.concat(newArgs) (or spread both) on every call.

checks.t: Binding does not call the function
checks.verify: let n = 0; function f() { n++ } const b = f.myBind(null); assert(n === 0, 'bind must not call the function'); b(); assert(n === 1, 'calling the bound function runs it once')
checks.gap: Return a function. Do not call the original inside myBind itself.

checks.t: The same bound function works for many calls
checks.verify:
function f(a, b) { return a + b } const b = f.myBind(null, 1);
assert(b(2) === 3 && b(3) === 4, 'partials must stay the same for each call')
checks.gap: Do not change the partials array (for example with push). Create a new joined array for each call.

checks.t: With new, the bound this is ignored
checks.verify:
function P(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y } const B = P.myBind({ ignored: true }, 1); const p = new B(2);
assert(p.x === 1 && p.y === 2, 'new must use partial and new arguments'); assert(p.ignored === undefined, 'bound this must be ignored with new'); assert(p instanceof P, 'instance must be instanceof the original')
checks.gap: Detect new with new.target. In that case build the object with Reflect.construct(target, args) and do not use thisArg.

checks.t: Instances can use methods from the original prototype
checks.verify:
function P(x) { this.x = x } P.prototype.double = function () { return this.x * 2 };
const B = P.myBind(null); assert(new B(4).double() === 8, 'instances must inherit from the original prototype')
checks.gap: Create the instance from the original function (Reflect.construct(target, args)), so it gets the original prototype.

checks.t: Calling myBind on a non-function throws a TypeError
checks.test:
try { Function.prototype.myBind.call({}) } catch (e) { console.log(e instanceof TypeError) }
// expected: true
checks.verify: let ok = false; try { Function.prototype.myBind.call({}) } catch (e) { ok = e instanceof TypeError } assert(ok, 'must throw TypeError')
checks.gap: At the start, check typeof this !== "function" and throw a TypeError.

notes: Save this in target first. Inside the returned function this means something else.
The new arguments go after the partials, and a fresh joined array is created on every call.
new.target is only defined when the function was called with new. That is the clean way to detect construction.
Reflect.construct(target, args) builds the object from the original function, so instanceof and prototype methods work.
The real bind also sets the name ("bound f") and length of the new function. That is a good extension.
next: Set bound.name to "bound " + target.name and subtract the partial count from length.
Implement Function.prototype.myCall and myApply without using call or apply (hint: a temporary property on an object).
Write partial(fn, ...args) that locks arguments but leaves this alone.
